Proof of a Crush
The label says CAL LOVES OWEN. Cal didn't write it. That doesn't make it wrong.
A collab loaf splits into a heart, a barista chalks it up as a confession, and the whole block wants an answer before the baker does.

Cal bakes next door to Owen's café, and their limited-edition loaf comes out of the oven with a heart-shaped crack. A barista labels it CAL LOVES OWEN, customers love it, and now two men who genuinely disagree about owning it have to sell bread under their own names. Over eight days of early shifts, tastings and one dinner neither of them cooks, you decide what Cal says out loud — and what he refuses to let a chalkboard say for him.
The café's barista — the one who chalked CAL LOVES OWEN on the label and now has to live with it.
If nobody speaks for himself, the customers will decide what Cal and Owen are, and neither of them gets to mean it.

An Expensive Label
Decide, in person, what happens to the label
The café window
Tuesday, 6:40 AM
In the café window, the collab loaf sits on a cake stand, its scored crust split open into a near-perfect heart.
Under it, in the barista's loopiest chalk: CAL LOVES OWEN. $14. Three customers have already photographed it. One took a selfie.
That's a very expensive label.
It's a scoring mark.
Sure. On my heart.
I pick the chalk up off the ledge and turn it over twice, like it might come with instructions.
It split in the oven. That's not a confession. That's steam.
Your call, baker. Half the block thinks it's adorable. The other half wants a wedding date.
What does Cal do with the label?
Wipe it and write the truth yourself.
I wipe the heart off and write, in block capitals: COLLAB SOURDOUGH. THE CRACK IS AN ACCIDENT. — CAL.
“Accident” is a strong word.
By noon, customers are asking which part was the accident. Cal doesn't answer. He does sell out.
Cal rewrote the label himself: collab sourdough, the heart-shaped crack an accident, signed with his name.
Let the joke stand today. No names tomorrow.
It stays till close. Tomorrow it says sourdough and nothing else.
A one-day romance. Very European of you.
Regulars leave paper hearts in the tip jar all day. Owen keeps the chalk in his apron pocket, like evidence.
Cal let the joke label stay for one day on the condition that tomorrow it names only the bread.
Pull the loaf. Your name isn't marketing.
I lift the loaf off the stand and carry it back through the connecting door.
My name goes on bread I made. Not on things I didn't say.
Fair. I'll have a word with the chalk artist.
The window stays empty until noon. Then Owen writes a new card himself, in plain print: SOURDOUGH. ASK THE BAKER.
Cal pulled the loaf from the window; Owen rewrote the card with no names on it.
Fighting the Dough
Knead together — and mind the distance
Whitaker's back kitchen
Wednesday, 4:20 AM
The ovens tick as they heat. Owen has shown up in a borrowed apron that says WHITAKER'S across his chest, which is its own problem.
I push the dough. It pushes back. I am losing a fight to flour and water in front of the one person who'd notice.
I watch his wrists for three full minutes. Then I wipe my hands and come around the bench.
Can I?
Please. It's winning.
I set my hands over his. Heel of the palm, push, fold, turn. His knuckles are warm. I keep my eyes on the dough.
You could just tell me.
I did. You kept fighting the dough.
Maybe it likes me back.
How close does Cal stay?
Stay. Guide him through one more fold.
One more fold. Then I step back, before one becomes two.
That was a very professional fold.
Tasting's tomorrow at six. Three loaves for the collab. Don't be polite about them.
Owen writes 6 AM on the back of his hand. He doesn't ask which loaf was made with him in mind. Cal doesn't say.
Cal guided Owen's hands with permission, stepped back on his own, and invited him to a six o'clock tasting.
Step back. Coach him from across the bench.
I let go and retreat to my side of the bench. Safer. Worse view.
Heel of the hand. Less wrestling. It isn't trying to escape.
Verbal instructions only. Very Victorian.
Tomorrow, six. Three flavors for the collab. You're my only taster, so try to have opinions.
Cal stepped back and coached Owen from across the bench, then asked him to be the only taster at six.
Take the dough. Finish it yourself.
I slide the dough away and finish it in four fast folds. Owen watches like it's a magic trick he's not allowed to learn.
Noted. Hands off the talent. I'm at least shaping my own.
His shaped loaf looks like a shoe. Cal bakes it anyway, on the good tray.
Come back at six tomorrow. I made three versions. I need someone who lies badly.
Cal took the dough back and finished it himself; Owen shaped his own lopsided loaf, and Cal still invited him to taste at six.
The Test Batch
Pick the real limited-edition flavor
Bakery counter, before opening
Thursday, 6:00 AM
Three loaves on a board: honey-lavender with pistachio, dark chocolate and sour cherry, and a plain country loaf with no card at all.
I slice all three. I don't explain the plain one. I baked it at 2 AM, while the fancy ones proved, because my hands needed something honest to do.
I try the lavender. The cherry. Polite nods. Then the plain one, and I stop talking for a second.
This one.
That's the test batch.
I like how it tastes before you try to impress me.
That's a sentence I'll be hearing at 3 AM for the rest of my life.
Which loaf goes on the limited menu?
Keep the plain one. Admit it's your favorite.
It's my favorite too. I just didn't think it was enough.
It's enough. It's the most enough thing on this board.
The limited run gets a plain card and a plain loaf. It sells out by ten. Nobody asks about hearts.
The plain country loaf became the limited edition; Cal admitted it was his favorite too.
Choose the cherry — and give the real reason.
Cherry. The plain one's mine. I don't want strangers deciding what it means.
I nod slowly. That's a better reason than any I would have guessed.
Cherry it is. Can I still have the plain one? Off the menu?
The window gets the cherry. A plain loaf waits in a paper bag behind the register, no name on it.
They launched the chocolate-cherry loaf; Cal kept the plain one off the menu and saved one for Owen.
Let sales decide what this is.
Put all three out. Whatever sells best is the answer. To everything.
I set the bread knife down.
No. I'm not letting a cash register answer for you. Pick bread, Cal. The other thing, you have to say.
They settle the menu with a coin flip. Cherry wins. Neither of them is proud of this.
Cal proposed letting sales decide everything; Owen refused to let sales stand in for an answer, and a coin flip picked the cherry loaf.
Sold Out Isn't a Yes
Keep customer hype from becoming a relationship fact
Café counter
Saturday, 2:10 PM
The limited loaf sold out at 1:58. Someone has posted a photo of the old label online: forty comments, and a proposed wedding hashtag.
I lift the SOLD OUT sign off its hook and prop it against the empty cake stand.
I rub out the last ghost of the old chalk and write the product name. Just the bread.
They loved the story.
They bought bread.
I know the difference.
Do you?
Then I'll ask you after closing.
That's a better time.
What does Cal do about “after closing”?
Name the time: six-fifteen, back door.
Six-fifteen. Back door. Leave the hashtag inside.
I'll put it in the tip jar.
A customer asks Cal point-blank if he's dating the coffee guy. Cal says, “Ask him after six,” and sells her a baguette.
Cal set a time to talk after closing, 6:15 at the back door, and told a curious customer to ask Owen, not the internet.
Ask for next week, when it's quiet.
Not tonight. Ask me when there isn't a line out the door and a hashtag.
Deal. I run a café. Waiting is basically my whole personality.
Owen tapes a note by the register: THE BREAD IS NOT A STATEMENT. It gets more likes than the wedding post.
Cal asked Owen to wait for a quieter week; Owen agreed and posted that the bread is not a statement.
Tell him there's nothing to ask.
There's nothing to ask, Owen. It's a crack in a crust.
I nod. It lands, and I let it.
Okay. Then I'll stop teasing. The bread's still great.
He doesn't tease once for the rest of the day. Cal notices the quiet more than he ever noticed the jokes.
Cal told Owen there was nothing to ask; Owen accepted it and stopped teasing.
Half Wrong
Find the first loaf Owen kept
The shared storeroom
Monday, 7:40 PM
After close, Cal goes looking for a proofing basket and finds a paper bag on Owen's shelf, folded twice, labeled in pen: DO NOT SELL.
Inside is Owen's first loaf from Wednesday. Lopsided, overproofed, scored like somebody sneezed. Wrapped like it matters.
You couldn't sell that.
I wasn't planning to.
I break off the heel, still more or less edible, and hold half of it out to him.
We eat it standing up. It's dense and a little sour. It's honestly not bad.
The label was only half wrong.
Which half?
What does Cal tell him?
Tell him the half that was right.
The part between the names. That part was right. I just wanted to be the one who said it.
I don't grin. I want to. I hold very still, like he's a loaf that might fall.
Thank you for saying it yourself.
Cal told Owen the “loves” part of the label was the true half, in his own words.
Say you'll answer somewhere without ovens.
Not in a storeroom. Somewhere that isn't work. Then I'll tell you which half.
Now I have to find a restaurant good enough for half a sentence.
Owen folds the bag closed again. He does not throw out the rest of the loaf.
Cal promised to say which half was true somewhere away from work; Owen kept the rest of the loaf.
Say the right half is your name.
The half with my name spelled right.
I laugh, because it's funny, and because he's allowed not to answer.
Fair. It's very well spelled.
Cal deflected with a joke about his name; Owen let him not answer.
No Ovens
Get an off-work dinner on the table
The alley behind both shops
Friday, 8:05 PM
The alley behind the two shops smells like spent espresso and burnt sugar. Owen sits on an upturned milk crate, apron already off.
Let me buy you dinner. Somewhere neither of us made a single thing.
No ovens. No customers.
Can I still criticize the bread?
Only if you kiss me after.
I say it lightly, so he can put it down lightly if he wants. Then I wait.
He left the door open. He always leaves the door open.
What does Cal say?
Say yes — criticism, kiss, all of it.
Yes. I'll be brutal about the bread. Then I'll kiss you.
That's the most romantic threat I've ever received.
They pick a Thai place four blocks down, specifically because its bread basket is famously terrible.
Cal said yes to dinner and, explicitly, to the kiss after.
Say yes to dinner. Leave the kiss off.
Dinner, yes. The kiss — not as a condition. Ask me that separately, later.
Separately. Got it. Dinner's still dinner.
Owen crosses something off an invisible list and doesn't sulk about it for one second. Cal notices that, too.
Cal accepted dinner without the kiss attached; Owen agreed to ask about it separately.
Say no. Not with terms, not tonight.
Not like this. Dinner shouldn't come with terms. Not even joking ones.
I stand and brush off my jeans. I don't make him say it twice.
Understood. No terms. The offer's open if you ever want one without any.
Cal turned down the dinner with the kiss attached; Owen withdrew it and left a no-terms offer open.
Somebody Else's Kitchen
Make a private invitation that stands apart from the collab
A small Thai restaurant, four blocks down
The following Thursday, 8:30 PM
Somebody else's kitchen, somebody else's rice. Cal flips the menu past the bread basket page without even looking.
I can keep one opinion to myself.
Only one?
I like you. That one stays out loud.
I set my fork down very carefully, like a man handling something that could still tip over.
Good. I like you too.
The run ends Sunday. The window, the label, the comments end with it. This doesn't have to.
Another dinner?
What is Cal actually asking for?
Ask for every Thursday — as a date.
No ovens required.
Every Thursday. As a date. Say it back so it counts.
Every Thursday. As a date. It counts.
Cal and Owen both said they like each other and agreed, out loud, to date every Thursday.
Ask to go slow. Bread speed.
I meant it. I just want to go slow. Bread speed, not espresso speed.
Bread speed. Overnight rises. I can do overnight.
They split the check down the middle, on purpose, and walk back the long way.
Cal said he likes Owen but wants to go slow; Owen agreed, and they kept dinners unhurried and undefined.
Say the timing's wrong. Honestly.
I like you. And from October to January I'm here at 3 AM. I won't give you the leftovers of that.
It stings. I let it. I don't argue him out of his own schedule.
Then no leftovers. We keep the collab. You keep your mornings.
Cal said he likes Owen but busy season leaves no room for dating; they chose to keep only the collaboration.
First Try
Say whether the label was true — or keep it to the bread
Whitaker's front window
Sunday, 5:45 AM — the last day of the run
Last day of the limited run. The chalkboard is blank, and the first regular is already peering through the glass.
I come through the connecting door with two coffees and say nothing about the blank board. It's his board.
Mrs. Alvarez, who has bought a baguette here every morning for six years, taps the window and mouths: Well? Is it true?
I pick up the chalk. The last loaf of the run cools on the rack behind me, scored plain. No heart.
Somebody else wrote the first version. This one's mine.
Whatever you write, I'm still bringing coffee tomorrow.
What does Cal write on the board?
Rename it “First Try.” Sit down with him.
I write FIRST TRY in block capitals. Underneath, smaller: Named by the baker. About the coffee guy. Confirmed.
You put a footnote on a confession.
It's accurate. Sit down. Your coffee's getting cold.
They eat the first slice at the window table, laughing at something nobody outside can hear. Mrs. Alvarez takes a picture. Owen asks her to post just the bread.
Cal renamed the loaf First Try and confirmed on the board, in his own words, that it was about Owen; they shared breakfast as a couple.
Write the bread's name. Keep the rest yours.
I write COUNTRY LOAF — LAST DAY. Nothing else. Mrs. Alvarez looks deeply betrayed.
Whatever this is, we name it. Not the window.
Agreed. Thursdays still Thursdays?
Thursdays stay.
Cal wrote only the bread's name; he and Owen kept working together and kept Thursdays, without letting customers define them.
Wrap him one plain loaf marked “Owen's.”
I wrap the last plain loaf, write OWEN'S on the paper, and hand it across the counter.
Busy season starts tomorrow. The collab stays. This is what I can give right now.
I take it with both hands, the way you take something that isn't small.
It's a good loaf, Cal. Thank you for not pretending it's more.
Cal chose busy season over romance, kept the collab, and gave Owen a plain loaf labeled OWEN'S; Owen accepted gracefully.
